“How to go from this, to this.”
Hook duration
3.4 seconds
Source views
473,621
OBSERVATION

The spoken opening promises a transformation. The body demonstrates the result and then moves into a tutorial. The contrast gives the viewer something concrete to compare.

TRY IN YOUR OWN EDIT

If your footage supports a before-and-after comparison, make the difference visible or audible first. Keep both versions comparable, then move directly into the explanation.

Spoken warningNo opening cut

A strong opening can
stay in one shot.

The spoken hook warns editors against sending a portfolio through Google Drive if they want to get hired.

Hook duration
4.9 seconds
Source views
488,152
OBSERVATION

This opening has no hard cut in the first three seconds. Later, a staged visual ladder compares different edits of the same line. Visual progress can happen inside a fixed composition.

TRY IN YOUR OWN EDIT

When the message is clear, consider letting one shot carry the opening. Use a relevant title or comparison to support the statement. A warning needs an explanation and a useful alternative.

A FAMILIAR CLIENT MOMENT
How much do you charge?
Here’s a way to frame the reply.
Start with the situation.Build the response.
Client situationNo opening cut

Start where your
audience already is.

The spoken opening addresses the moment a client asks an editor for a price, then promises an alternative response.

Hook duration
4.1 seconds
Source views
310,113
OBSERVATION

The video begins with a specific situation. Its body builds a message conversation bubble by bubble, using the conversation itself to show progression within a mostly fixed shot.

TRY IN YOUR OWN EDIT

Choose a moment your audience recognizes, then make the response readable in small steps. Keep the text focused on the line being discussed instead of showing the whole conversation at once.
